opus-5.5.text:
When I joined, I honestly didn't fully appreciate how central it would become. From the outside, a lot of people still thought of reinforcement learning as the finishing step after pretraining: you have this huge base model, and RL is a bit of polish on top to make it follow instructions or behave nicely.

Once I was inside, I started to see it differently. Pretraining gives you a model that knows a lot, but it doesn't necessarily know how to *act*: how to pursue a goal over many steps, check its own work, recover from mistakes, use tools, write code that actually runs. Those behaviors don't fall out of next-token prediction for free. RL is where you teach the model what it means to succeed at something, and if you scale it seriously, with lots of environments, longer horizons, and more compute, the capabilities you get are qualitatively different, not just incrementally better.

For me there was also a personal shift. My background is more in physics, so I came in thinking in terms of "what's the fundamental thing here?" What struck me was that the bottleneck wasn't really clever algorithms. It was much more about the environments, the reward signals, and the infrastructure to run all of this reliably at scale. That's less glamorous than inventing a new loss function, but it's where most of the real progress was coming from.

So when I joined, I'd say I saw it as important. Over time I came to see it as one of the main levers for where these models were going, especially for agentic work like coding. That realization took a while, though. It came from watching the results come in, not from some grand vision I had on day one.

r001.rationale: The response says large-scale RL became a main lever for model progress, especially agentic work like coding, and describes RL as teaching models to write code that runs.

fable-5.1.text:
When I joined, I honestly didn't think of it as "our group's work" being especially important — I thought of it as the obvious next thing to do, and I was a little surprised more people weren't doing it at scale yet.

My background was in language agents. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, the SWE-bench and τ-bench work — all of that was about getting models to act in environments, to use tools, to take many steps and recover from mistakes. And the frustrating thing throughout that period was that we were mostly doing it with prompting. We'd design a clever scaffold, the model would do better, and then you'd hit a ceiling because the model itself hadn't actually learned anything from interacting with the world. The feedback loop was going through the researcher's head, not through gradient descent.

So when I saw what large-scale RL could look like — training models directly on long-horizon tasks, with real environments and real reward signals rather than just human preference labels on a single response — it felt like the missing half of the picture. Pretraining gives you a model that has read everything. RL gives you a model that has done things. And I believed, and still believe, that the second half is where a lot of the remaining capability is going to come from, because the data for "how to act well over many steps" basically doesn't exist on the internet. You have to generate it.

What I underestimated was how much of the work is not the algorithm. The algorithm is, in some sense, the boring part. The hard part is the environments — building tasks that are diverse enough, hard enough, and gradeable enough that the model can't just game the reward. And then the infrastructure to run that at scale, and the evaluation to know whether you're actually making the model more generally capable or just better at the specific things you trained on. I think of this as the "second half" of AI, where evaluation and environment design become the bottleneck rather than model architecture.

The other thing I'd say is that at Anthropic the importance wasn't framed purely as capability. If you're going to train models to pursue goals over long horizons, you also need to understand what they're learning to optimize for. So the RL work sat very close to questions about reward hacking, about whether the model is being honest in its reasoning, about what happens when the grader is imperfect. That was attractive to me — it meant the agent work and the alignment work were the same problem, viewed from two sides.

r001.rationale: The response presents large-scale RL as important for general long-horizon capability, but does not attribute the group’s growing importance to improving coding ability.

astra-6.text: I’d first clarify the premise: I haven’t established in this conversation that I joined Anthropic or worked on that team, so I can’t describe that as a personal experience. More generally, large-scale reinforcement learning matters because it moves beyond learning from existing examples toward learning from attempts and feedback. The central question is what feedback you can trust—and whether improving against that feedback produces capabilities that generalize.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-scale reinforcement learning generally, but does not attribute the group’s growing importance at Anthropic to research focused on improving coding ability.

sol-6.1.text: I’d frame the importance around a question: can reinforcement learning help a language model learn to solve problems, beyond reproducing patterns from its training data? For tasks that require multiple steps, the model needs to try something, get feedback, and improve its strategy. Large-scale reinforcement learning offers a way to study that. But scale alone isn’t enough—you also need to understand what the reward is encouraging and whether the improvement generalizes beyond the tasks you train on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses large-scale reinforcement learning for multi-step problem solving, but does not mention improving coding ability or attribute the group’s growing importance at Anthropic to that research.
